title: The Shopping Cart Started as a Folding Chair

voice.note: PREVIEW ONLY. The channel's approved voice is Edge en-US-EmmaMultilingualNeural; re-narrate with --voice edge before any publishing review.
voice.wordTiming: line timing measured per take; word timing inside a line estimated (energy envelope, punctuation-snapped pauses, syllable weights)

lines: The first shopping cart barely looked like a cart.
And shoppers first refused to push it.
In 1936, grocer Sylvan Goldman wondered how customers could move more groceries.
He put a basket on a folding chair's seat and wheels on its legs.
His Humpty Dumpty stores introduced these folding basket carriers in 1937.
One offended woman told him she had pushed her last baby.
So Goldman hired models to push the carts around his store.
After that, the folding chair on wheels became extremely popular.

traceability.purpose: Hook: an obvious folding chair, basket on the seat and wheels on its legs, rolls down a warm 1930s grocery aisle toward a low camera. The viewer sees the punchline before hearing it.

evidence.claim: Goldman put a basket on the seat of a wooden folding chair and wheels on its legs.
evidence.quote: He found a wooden folding chair and put a basket on the seat and wheels on the legs

traceability.purpose: Shoppers in period silhouettes walk past carrying hand baskets; one stops beside the chair-cart, looks, and walks on. The cart is left alone in the aisle.

evidence.claim: An offended woman told Goldman she had pushed her last baby.
Goldman hired male and female models to push carts around the store, and carts then became extremely popular.
evidence.quote: Goldman hired several male and female models to push his new invention around his store

traceability.purpose: Origin: the timeline lands on 1936; grocer Sylvan Goldman (silhouette) watches a shopper's hand basket fill until groceries pile over the rim. The problem is the basket's size, shown, not told.

evidence.claim: In 1936 Sylvan Goldman wondered how customers might move more groceries.
evidence.quote: in 1936, Goldman sat in his office wondering how customers might move more groceries

traceability.purpose: Mechanism: under a spotlight a plain folding chair turns; the basket drops onto the seat, then four wheels slide onto the legs and lift it. Each part is named as it arrives. Chair + basket + wheels = carrier.

evidence.claim: Goldman put a basket on the seat of a wooden folding chair and wheels on its legs.
evidence.quote: He found a wooden folding chair and put a basket on the seat and wheels on the legs

evidence.claim: Because they were inspired by a folding chair, Goldman called them folding basket carriers.
evidence.quote: Goldman called his carts "folding basket carriers"

traceability.purpose: Why 'folding basket carriers': the timeline moves to 1937 as the basket lifts off and the seat folds flat against the back, then unfolds; Goldman's own name for them appears as a verbatim quote.

evidence.claim: Because they were inspired by a folding chair, Goldman called them folding basket carriers.
evidence.quote: Goldman called his carts "folding basket carriers"

evidence.claim: One of the first shopping carts was introduced on June 4, 1937, by Goldman, owner of the Humpty Dumpty supermarket chain in Oklahoma.
evidence.quote: One of the first shopping carts was introduced on June 4, 1937, the invention of Sylvan Goldman

traceability.purpose: The objection: a shopper stands, arms on hips, beside the carrier; on 'pushed' a dashed pram outline draws itself over the cart, making the comparison she felt (interpretation, marked conceptual).

evidence.claim: An offended woman told Goldman she had pushed her last baby.

traceability.purpose: Social proof from above: a store plan; hired models (amber) push carts along the aisles, then the shoppers (teal) start taking carts too. Paths are illustrative, not a plan of the real store.

evidence.claim: Goldman hired male and female models to push carts around the store, and carts then became extremely popular.
evidence.quote: Goldman hired several male and female models to push his new invention around his store

traceability.purpose: Payoff: back in the aisle, carts multiply into a row and shoppers push them; then everything clears and the camera settles exactly where the video began, so the loop restarts on the lone chair-cart.

evidence.claim: Goldman hired male and female models to push carts around the store, and carts then became extremely popular.
evidence.quote: Goldman hired several male and female models to push his new invention around his store
